title: Search Jerusalem for One Just Person
summary: God sends Jeremiah through Jerusalem's streets to find a single person who acts justly and seeks truth, promising to forgive the city if he does. Neither the poor nor the powerful pass the test. The people have grown fat on deceit, ignored the orphan and the needy, dismissed the prophets as wind, and forgotten the God who sets the sea its boundary and sends the rain. A distant, ancient nation will come, though God will not make a full end.
story: Chapter 4 sounded the alarm of invasion. Chapter 5 explains why it must come, and it does so by going looking. The scene recalls Abraham bargaining with God over Sodom (Genesis 18:22-33), where God agreed to spare the city for ten righteous people; here the number has dropped to one, and still no one is found. The chapter moves from the city's streets to its homes, its courts, and its temple, and at each level finds the same refusal to listen. It adds a new element to the charge: not only idolatry but injustice to the poor, a theme that will grow in the temple sermon of chapter 7.
historical:
The chapter is poetry without a date, and most scholars place it with chapters 4 and 6 in the years when the threat from the north was taking shape, whether late in Josiah's reign or under Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC). The social picture fits what is known of Jehoiakim's time. Jeremiah 22:13-17 condemns that king for building a lavish palace with unpaid labor while shedding innocent blood, and verses 26 to 28 here describe a wealthy class grown rich on deceit.

Verse 15 describes the invader as an ancient and established nation with a language Judah does not understand. That fits Babylon, whose culture and cities went back thousands of years and whose language, Akkadian, was unintelligible to Hebrew speakers, though Aramaic was increasingly the shared language of diplomacy. The description echoes the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:49, which warned of a nation from afar whose language Israel would not understand.
cultural:
Oaths were a pillar of ancient life, sworn in courts, contracts, and daily dealings. Swearing As surely as the LORD lives called God to witness that a statement was true. Verse 2 says the people used this oath while lying, which made God himself the guarantor of their falsehood. Verse 1's streets and squares were the public places of an ancient city, where business, gossip, and legal cases happened at the gates.

The fowlers of verses 26 and 27 were bird-catchers who used nets, snares, and decoys, and kept the birds in wicker cages to sell. Jeremiah pictures the rich filling their houses with the profits of deceit the way a fowler fills a cage. Israel's law required special care for the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner, who had no male protector in a society organized around households (Deuteronomy 24:17-22), and to neglect their cause in court was a basic covenant failure. Verse 24 refers to the autumn and spring rains that bracketed the growing season and to the appointed weeks of harvest, the seven weeks from the barley harvest to the wheat harvest that ended in the Feast of Weeks.
literary: The chapter is poetry built around a repeated refrain: Should I not punish them for these things? Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this? (verses 9 and 29). The refrain divides the chapter into sections, each laying out evidence and then asking the same question, as a judge might ask a jury. The first section is a search (verses 1 to 6) in which Jeremiah tries the poor and then the powerful. The central section answers the people's claim that God will do nothing (verses 12 and 13) with the reply that God's words in Jeremiah's mouth will be a fire. Verses 21 to 24 draw on creation, contrasting the obedient sea, which never crosses its boundary, with a people who cross every boundary God set. The chapter ends with a question pointed at the hearers: what will you do in the end?

outline.t: Not one just person, poor or powerful
They say God will do nothing: a distant nation is coming
The sea obeys, but this people does not
Rich through deceit; prophets and priests who lie

doctrines.note: Sin in this chapter is social as much as religious. False oaths, adultery, deceit in business, and neglect of the fatherless and needy all belong to the same rebellion. The people's faces are harder than stone, and they have eyes but do not see.

The refrain, Should I not punish them, shows judgment as the just response of a God who has warned and disciplined without effect. Yet God limits it: he will not make a full end, and he tells Judah the reason for the exile so they can understand it.

God points to the sand that holds back the sea and to the rains that come in their season. The ordered world is evidence of the Creator's power and generosity, and ingratitude for it is part of Judah's guilt.

words.note: Emunah, faithfulness or truth, from the root meaning firm or reliable. In verse 1 God seeks someone who seeks emunah, and in verse 3 Jeremiah says God's eyes look for it. It means integrity in word and deed, being someone who can be relied on. The same word appears in Habakkuk 2:4, the righteous will live by his faithfulness.

Salach, to forgive or pardon, a verb used in the Old Testament only with God as the subject. God offers to forgive the city if one just person is found (verse 1), and then asks, Why should I forgive you (verse 7). Forgiveness is always God's to give, and he longs to give it; the question is whether the people will accept it.

Musar, discipline, correction, or instruction, the word often translated instruction in Proverbs. Verse 3 says God struck the people, but they refused to accept discipline. Hardship was meant as a father's correction to turn them back; they felt no pain and learned nothing.

Din, judgment, cause, or legal claim. Verse 28 says the rich have not taken up the cause of the fatherless. In Israel the powerful were expected to secure justice for the weak in court; failing to do so was not a private lapse but a public betrayal of the covenant.

christ: The search for one just person who could save a city is answered, in the New Testament's reading of the whole biblical story, by Jesus the righteous one whose obedience brings life to many (Romans 5:18-19; 1 Peter 3:18). This is a theological connection rather than a prediction in the chapter: Jeremiah's point is that no one was found. Jesus also takes up the language of verse 21 about having eyes but not seeing and ears but not hearing (Mark 8:18; compare Isaiah 6:9-10), applying it to those, including his own disciples, who failed to understand him. His teaching about wealth and the poor, and his warnings to religious leaders, continue Jeremiah's insistence that faithfulness to God cannot be separated from justice for the weak.

hard.q: Was there really not one just person in Jerusalem? What about Jeremiah himself?
hard.a:
The chapter says God will forgive the city if even one person who acts justly can be found, and none is. Yet the book itself knows faithful people: Jeremiah, his secretary Baruch, the officials who protected him (26:24), Ebed-melech who rescued him from the cistern (38:7-13), and presumably others. Interpreters handle this in a few ways. Many take the search as prophetic hyperbole, deliberate exaggeration that exposes the corruption of the city as a whole, like the psalmist's cry that no one does good (Psalm 14:3). Others note that Jeremiah is the searcher, not one of the searched, and that the test is aimed at the city's public life, its courts and marketplaces, where the few faithful had no influence.

Others see the point theologically: the lack of even one righteous person shows that the problem is not a few bad leaders but the heart of the people, which is why the book will later promise a new covenant that changes hearts (31:33). On any reading, the chapter's force is not in counting heads but in showing a society where injustice had become normal.

questions: If someone searched your town or church for a person who acts justly and seeks truth, what would they be looking for? Would they find it in you?
The people said God would do nothing. In what ways do people today assume that God will not act or that consequences will never come?
The chapter ties faithfulness to God to caring for the fatherless and needy. How are those two connected in your own life?
